title: Contemplation is waking up
hook: for Merton, contemplation is being fully awake to the life you've been given
tomorrow: the false self and the true self

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vigils: monks singing psalms in the dark before dawn. Your line was pray before the world wakes. Did you try the early five minutes? Today, the waking itself. Day two hundred seventy-seven.

You've driven home and realized you don't remember a single turn. You've eaten a whole meal and couldn't say what it tasted like. You've sat with someone you love and been somewhere else entirely. We spend a lot of life on autopilot. Most of us assume the spiritual life is about adding something extra on top: more prayers, more feelings, more effort. Thomas Merton said something stranger. The deepest prayer isn't adding anything. It's waking up to what's already here. Today: contemplation.
screen: `HOME, AND YOU DON'T REMEMBER THE DRIVE.` → `LIFE ON AUTOPILOT.` → `WAKING UP TO WHAT'S HERE.`

segments.voice: First, Merton's definition. In New Seeds of Contemplation, from 1961, he calls contemplation the highest expression of our spiritual life, and then he says what it is: that same life, wide awake and aware that it's alive. A kind of spiritual wonder, he says, a deep gratitude for being. Not a trance. Not a special feeling. Not an escape from the world. Awake. Second, you can't force a waking. Merton describes it as an awakening to the real in everything that is real, and he's clear that no method switches it on. Think of how mornings work. You can't wake yourself up by trying harder. But you can open the curtains, put the phone in another room, stop hitting snooze. Silence, prayer and attention are the curtains. The waking comes when it comes. Third, not only for monks. Merton's first version of this book, Seeds of Contemplation, came out in 1949, written very much from inside the cloister. When he reworked it twelve years later, he widened the door. A parent at the stove can be awake. So can a student on a bus. So could the old farmer at Ars you met a few weeks ago, looking and being looked at. Fourth, the old wake-up call. Saint Paul quotes what may be an early Christian hymn, in the Douay-Rheims: "Rise thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead: and Christ shall enlighten thee." The Greek verb for rise there is the same one used for raising the dead. For Merton, the sleep isn't at night. It's the half-attention we live in all day. Waking up is the prayer, and it can start with the next thing you do, done with your whole self.
screen: `LIFE ITSELF, WIDE AWAKE.` · `YOU CAN'T FORCE A WAKING.` · `NOT ONLY FOR MONKS.` · `RISE THOU THAT SLEEPEST.` · then, large: `WAKING UP IS THE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wake up to one thing. Pick something right in front of you: your hands, a cup, the window. Look at it as if you'd never seen it. Its color. Its weight. The light on it. When your mind drifts off to plans, notice, and come back. Then feel your own breathing, and let yourself know: I'm alive, right now. That's it. If you pray, you can simply stay there, awake, in God's presence. The bell holds the time.
Egeire. The Greek word for 'rise' or 'wake up,' also used for raising the dead, and for Merton, the deepest prayer: being fully awake to the life you've been given. Today's word.
Your line: wake up. Today, choose one ordinary thing, washing a dish, walking to the car, a cup of coffee, and do it fully awake, with nothing else going. Day two hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics practice contemplative prayer in many forms, from silent time before the Blessed Sacrament to centering prayer and lectio divina, and the Catechism describes contemplation as a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus.

fork.setup: you're Merton, twelve years after your first book on contemplation, written inside the cloister. reworking it, who do you say it's for?
options: anyone, inside the cloister or out
fork.reveal: New Seeds widens the door: waking up to your own life isn't reserved for the monastery.

original.note: Greek: wake up, sleeper (Ephesians 5:14). egeire is also the verb for raising the dead.

trapdoor: what you thought: contemplation is thinking hard about something.
what it means: for Merton, being fully awake to the life you've been given, with wonder and gratitude.
what a scholar hears: Seeds (1949) reworked as New Seeds (1961); 'an awakening to the Real'; and egeire in Ephesians 5:14, the verb of resurrection.
